exercise.name: Lever Single Arm Chest Press (plate loaded)

reference.title: Lever Single Arm Chest Press (plate loaded)
reference.listing: Video (movement reference only; the page could not be fetched from the authoring environment (gymvisual.com refused the request), so the data sheet was not read and the movement follows the exercise name and standard coaching)

breathing.pattern: Breathe in as the handle comes back, breathe out as you press.
breathing.cadence: About 2 s back, short pause, about 1.3 s press

prescription.effort: Stop 1-3 reps short of failure (RIR 1-3, clinical opinion)
prescription.load: Plate load is user-chosen: start with light plates on the horns and press with the back on the pad.
prescription.progression: Add reps, then a small plate; slower return

cues.text: Sit with the back on the pad and both feet flat; right hand on the right handle, left hand resting on the left thigh; arm extended, palm down.
Breathe in and let the handle come back beside the chest on its arc, elbow about 45-60 degrees from the trunk.
Pause with the hand beside the chest; keep both shoulders on the pad and the hips square.
Breathe out and press the handle forward until the arm is long; do not let the trunk twist toward the handle.
Squeeze the chest with the arm long; switch sides after the set.

mistakes.mistake: Trunk twisting toward the working side
mistakes.fix: Keep both shoulder blades on the pad; lighten the load.
Keep the elbow about 45-60 degrees from the trunk.

mistakes.mistake: Shoulder rolling forward at the end
mistakes.fix: Stop with the arm long and the shoulder blade on the pad.
Take about 2 s to bring the handle back.

kinematics.norm: From well bent with the hands beside the chest to nearly straight (clinical opinion)
About 45-60 degrees from the trunk at the chest (clinical opinion)
Pronated: palm down on a horizontal handle (clinical opinion)
The right handle rides its own lever arc; only the working lever is shown (clinical opinion)
Back on the pad, little trunk work compared with free-weight or standing presses (Saeterbakken and Fimland 2012)
Unilateral pressing asks more of the trunk muscles than bilateral pressing (Saeterbakken and Fimland 2012)
Controlled, about 2 s back and 1-1.5 s press (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #14232, Lever Single Arm Chest Press (plate loaded), video (movement reference)
Saeterbakken & Fimland 2012, muscle activity of the core during bilateral, unilateral, seated and standing resistance exercise (Eur J Appl Physiol 112:1671-1678)

Saeterbakken, van den Tillaar and Fimland 2011, a comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements (J Sports Sci 29(5):533-538; PubMed 21225489)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
Load is user-chosen: start light and press without the back leaving the pad.
At the end of the set let the handles come back under control before letting go.
Load the plates on the working arm only and keep the other arm clear of the resting lever.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Shoulder discomfort: shorten the range so the hands stop in front of the chest.
Low back discomfort: keep both feet flat and the back on the pad.
progressions: Slower return with a pause at the chest.

muscleNotes.pec_r: Prime mover: pushes the arm forward and across.
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Flexes the shoulder with the chest.
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Moves the shoulder blade forward at the end of the press.
muscleNotes.core: Holds the trunk square on the pad.
muscleNotes.biceps_r: Controls the elbow on the return.
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Resist the twist of a one-arm press (Saeterbakken and Fimland 2012).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Resist the twist of a one-arm press (Saeterbakken and Fimland 2012).
